clue.text: One who wants no help to make: advances, we hear — Don Juan

indicators.note: we hear tells the solver that the word for advances is to be taken as it is spoken

parts.note: advances of money are loans
a Don Juan is a womaniser, slang a wolf

explanation.surface: Someone who refuses help makes his own advances, like a seducer on the prowl.
explanation.walkthrough: LOAN (advances) said aloud gives LONE; WOLF is a predatory womaniser.
explanation.definitionFit: A loner who prefers to act independently, refusing assistance, is called this.

clue.text: Look, it's the turn of English restaurants to be humiliated

parts.note: lo is an old word meaning look

indicators.note: the turn of says the letters for English restaurants are read backwards

parts.note: cafes are simple restaurants

explanation.surface: It is England's restaurants' turn to suffer embarrassment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the turn of' reverses the abbreviation and the eateries together, giving SEFACE. 'humiliated' looks like the definition alone, but 'be' belongs with it so the swap is a verb phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: To lose face is to suffer humiliation or loss of respect.

clue.text: I'm a chief myself

explanation.surface: A leader introduces themself.
explanation.walkthrough: The first phrase means the top person, the boss; the second is the informal term for oneself, as in looking after this person first.
explanation.definitionFit: The head person or leader is so called, and the phrase is also a jokey term for oneself.

clue.text: Outlawed old stretch of forest

indicators.note: out signals that the letters which follow it in the same word are put out of order

explanation.surface: A banned ancient tract of woodland.
explanation.walkthrough: The device splits Outlawed into OUT, the anagram signal, and LAWED, which it rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: The Weald of south-east England was once a great forest; the name comes from an Old English word for woodland.

clue.text: One's behind a horse covered in grease

indicators.note: covered in says the horse piece is wrapped by the grease word

parts.note: lard is pig fat, a grease
GG, gee-gee, is a child's word for a horse

explanation.surface: A rider trails behind a horse smeared in fat.
explanation.definitionFit: A laggard is someone who falls behind or lags.

clue.text: Party leading the field

parts.note: a do is a party
main means chief or leading

explanation.surface: A political party is ahead of the rest of the field.
explanation.definitionFit: A domain is a sphere of activity or knowledge, a field.

clue.text: Give short change in error

indicators.note: change tells the solver to reorder the letters of Give short

explanation.surface: Short-changing a customer by mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short change' looks like a phrase; 'change' is the anagram signal for GIVE SHORT.
explanation.definitionFit: An oversight is a mistake made by failing to notice something.

clue.text: Stay in Lincoln — I would!

indicators.note: in places the shortened I would inside the president's name

parts.note: Abe is the first name of Abraham Lincoln
I'd is the contraction of I would

explanation.surface: Someone enthusiastically says they would stay in the city of Lincoln.
explanation.walkthrough: Lincoln looks like the English city; it is Abraham (ABE) Lincoln, the US president.
explanation.definitionFit: To abide is to remain or stay somewhere.

clue.text: Cleopatra's sewer

parts.note: sewer means one who sews, a stitching tool, not a drain; the obelisk on the Thames Embankment bears Cleopatra's name and the same tool's name

explanation.surface: The Egyptian queen's drain.
explanation.walkthrough: Sewer reads as a drain; it is something that sews. Cleopatra's Needle is an ancient Egyptian obelisk in London.
explanation.definitionFit: The sharp sewing implement shares its name with the London obelisk called Cleopatra's Needle.

clue.text: The French people aren't extremely keen

parts.note: la is a French word for the
men are people
the extremity, or tail end, of the word aren't is its closing letter

explanation.surface: French people are not particularly enthusiastic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'keen' looks like the adjective for eager; it is the verb to wail in grief. 'aren't extremely' gives T, the letter at the word's far end.
explanation.definitionFit: To keen is to wail in mourning, so it means to mourn aloud.

clue.text: Pacific islands give it the bird

parts.note: it is old slang for sex appeal, abbreviated SA
the moa is an extinct flightless New Zealand bird

explanation.surface: Someone tells the Pacific islands to dismiss or jeer at something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Give it the bird' looks like an idiom for jeering; instead 'it' is SA (sex appeal) and the bird is the MOA.
explanation.definitionFit: Samoa is an island group in the South Pacific.

clue.text: Must we get out of this communication system?

definitions.text: Must we get out of this communication system?

parts.words: Must we get out of this communication system?
parts.note: must is unfermented grape juice, which we get from the plant that bears grapes; that plant is also the informal word-of-mouth network of gossip

explanation.surface: Someone trapped in an unpleasant network asks whether escape is compulsory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Must' reads as a verb, but it is the noun for fresh grape juice.
explanation.definitionFit: The rumour mill, where news spreads by informal word of mouth, is named after a climbing fruit plant.

clue.text: Shame on you, Alfred, corrupting a bird

parts.note: fie is an old exclamation of disapproval, shame on you

indicators.note: corrupting means spoiling the letters of Alfred into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone scolds Alfred for leading a girl astray.
explanation.walkthrough: 'corrupting' rearranges the name to give LDFARE. 'a bird' looks like it could be a separate piece, but the 'a' belongs to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The fieldfare is a large thrush that visits Britain in winter.

clue.text: A hard case in the classroom

explanation.surface: A tough pupil causes trouble at school.
explanation.walkthrough: At some English public schools a shell is an intermediate form, or class, between years.
explanation.definitionFit: A tortoise or nut has a tough protective covering, and at certain English schools the word also names a form or class.

clue.text: Hit a century, made fast

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, a century
made fast means secured, locked

explanation.surface: A batsman scores a hundred runs, and quickly too.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads like cricket, where a century is 100 runs; 'fast' means secure, not quick.
explanation.definitionFit: Clocked is slang for struck, as in punched someone.

clue.text: Derelict dock in familiar surroundings going cheap

indicators.note: surroundings says the familiar word goes around the jumbled letters

parts.note: known means familiar

indicators.note: derelict means ruined, so dock is broken up

explanation.surface: An abandoned dock in a well-known area is for sale at a low price.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Derelict' scrambles the four-letter harbour word to CKDO, and 'surroundings' wraps the familiar word around it. 'going cheap' is the definition, as in a knockdown price.
explanation.definitionFit: A knockdown price is a very low one, so goods offered at it are going cheaply.

clue.text: Temptress finally put on figure — hugging garment

indicators.note: put on says the letter is placed after the other piece

parts.note: printed as figure-hugging, meaning close-fitting, tight

indicators.note: finally says to take only the closing letter of Temptress

explanation.surface: A seductress at last pulls on a clinging dress.
explanation.walkthrough: The page prints 'figure-hugging' split across a line; it gives TIGHT, with S, the last letter of Temptress, put on the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Tights are a close-fitting legwear item worn from waist to feet.

clue.text: Small sketch, perhaps, showing leaf spike

parts.note: to thumb is to leaf through pages
a nail is a metal spike

explanation.surface: A tiny drawing shows a pointed leaf.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaf' looks like a noun; it is the verb to turn pages.
explanation.definitionFit: A thumbnail sketch is a brief outline or miniature drawing; perhaps signals one example.

clue.text: Right to succeed

explanation.surface: A person has the entitlement to prosper.
explanation.definitionFit: To put a wrong right is to repair it, and to prosper is to do well in life.

clue.text: Ask somebody to beat it

parts.note: to beg is to ask earnestly
one means somebody, as in one never knows

explanation.surface: A person is told to request that someone go away.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue reads as one instruction, but 'beat it' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An old-fashioned command to go away, equivalent to the slang order to clear off.

clue.text: Catch in Antwerp on the loose without wife

indicators.note: on the loose means freed, so the remaining letters run riot
without says a letter is dropped from Antwerp

explanation.surface: Trying to catch an escapee in Antwerp while the wife stays home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' removes W from ANTWERP; 'on the loose' rearranges ANTERP.
explanation.definitionFit: To entrap is to snare or trick someone into a trap.

clue.text: Something that's essential when turning orange

indicators.note: turning says the whole run of letters is read in the opposite direction

parts.note: a must is something essential, so a must
as means when, as in as I left

explanation.surface: Something vital happens when a piece of fruit changes colour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turning' reverses A MUST AS to give the fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: A satsuma is a type of mandarin, a small loose-skinned citrus fruit.

clue.text: Paid out about a sovereign for an instrument once

indicators.note: about says the money word goes round the royal letters

parts.note: spent means paid out
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is a sovereign

explanation.surface: Someone paid a gold coin for an old musical instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sovereign' suggests the gold coin; it is ER, the Queen.
explanation.definitionFit: The serpent was an old snake-shaped bass wind instrument.

clue.text: Remains in rows

explanation.surface: Leftovers are arranged in lines.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rows' rhymes with cows here: quarrels.
explanation.definitionFit: Leftover bits of food are scraps, and fights or quarrels are also scraps.

clue.text: Pot a large animal, by the sound of it

indicators.note: by the sound of it says the word for the animal is heard rather than spelt

parts.note: croc is short for crocodile, a large reptile

explanation.surface: Someone shoots a big beast, as one might hear it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pot' looks like the verb to shoot game; it is the definition, an earthenware jar.
explanation.definitionFit: An earthenware jar or vessel is called this.

clue.text: Novelist makes killer and last two characters change places.

parts.note: orc is another name for the killer whale

indicators.note: change places means the pair swap round

parts.note: the final pair of the alphabet are Y and Z

explanation.surface: A writer creates a murderer, and the final two letters swap.
explanation.walkthrough: Baroness Orczy wrote The Scarlet Pimpernel.
explanation.definitionFit: Baroness Emma Orczy was the author of The Scarlet Pimpernel.

clue.text: Vessel in race round island — it takes the record

indicators.note: in says the vessel word sits inside the race word

parts.note: the TT is the Tourist Trophy motorcycle race on the Isle of Man
an urn is a vessel

indicators.note: round says the island name is turned about

parts.note: Elba is the Mediterranean island of Napoleon's exile

explanation.surface: A boat competes in a race around an island and sets a record.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round' turns the Mediterranean island into ABLE. The TT is the Isle of Man motorcycle race; 'it takes the record' describes the spinning platform of a record player.
explanation.definitionFit: The rotating platform of a record player holds the disc.

clue.text: Recorder has to come to the point

explanation.surface: A tape machine must make a point.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recorder' looks like the instrument; it is one who tapes. 'come to the point' means narrow to a tip.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who makes tapes is so called, and to narrow gradually to a tip is to taper.

clue.text: Make a charge on roads

indicators.note: make says the letters of the words a charge on are formed into something new

explanation.surface: An instruction to levy a toll on highways.
explanation.walkthrough: 'roads' looks like highways but is the nautical term for sheltered water where ships ride at anchor.
explanation.definitionFit: Roads, or a roadstead, is a sheltered stretch of water where ships can moor.

clue.text: Softly-softly, lad, with a ring

parts.note: p is the musical abbreviation for ..., softly
Ian is a boy's name, a lad
O is shaped like a ring

explanation.surface: A gentle approach is used by a young man with a ring, perhaps proposing.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed 'Softly-softly' gives two pieces: the first half is the definition, the second gives P.
explanation.definitionFit: In music the Italian term is the direction to play quietly.

clue.text: Gnome always to be found in grass

indicators.note: to be found in says one word sits inside the other

parts.note: to grass, or sing, is to inform to the police
ay is a poetic word for always

explanation.surface: A garden ornament is forever lying in the lawn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gnome' suggests a garden figure; here it means a pithy saying, and 'grass' means to inform.
explanation.definitionFit: A gnome is a short pithy maxim, an aphorism.

clue.text: In the beginning, was first made to jump

parts.note: a start is a beginning
led means was in front, was first

explanation.surface: At the outset, someone was the first person made to leap.
explanation.definitionFit: To be startled is to be given a sudden fright that makes one flinch.
